newsitem.title: CHINA: Drought kills harvest hopes in hungry North Korea.
newsitem.headline: Drought kills harvest hopes in hungry North Korea.

text.p: Devastating drought across North Korea has extinguished all hope that autumn harvests will end food shortages which have caused malnutrition among more than a third of all children, aid workers said on Monday.

Corn and rice plants were wilting in parched fields across the isolated Stalinist nation, prompting officials to grant unprecedented access to agencies helping to feed their hungry people, officials of the Oxfam aid agency said.

The drought, coming after two years of flooding that wrecked North Korea's irrigation systems, meant the food crisis would intensify and persist well into 1998, said Tricia Parker, programme director of Oxfam Hong Kong.

"We were told several times that...people had hoped that with this harvest they would get back on their own feet again -- but they can see now that, because of the effects of the drought, that will not happen," Parker told a news conference in Beijing after returning from a 10-day visit to North Korea.
"The harvest will come in September and October, but we now know that it will certainly not be enough food to see the Korean people through the next 12 months," she said.

Even before Pyongyang this summer reported its worst heatwave for 61 years, international aid workers had predicted that severe shortages of seed, fuel and fertiliser meant the grain harvest would be far below the 7.4 million tonnes needed.
Early estimates by crop experts suggested that drought had destroyed 50 percent of the North Korean corn crop, with about 15 percent of the rice crop also damaged, Oxfam officials said.

Rivers were running dry and in some corn fields yields were likely to reach only about 500 kg per hectare (446 lb per acre) -- a fraction of the normal three to four tonnes (1,800-2,700 lb per acre), said emergency officer Teddy Arellano.

Health officials reported that around 600,000 children aged up to five, or 38 percent of the total, were malnourished, and thin and listless infants were a common sight in North Korea's neat and well-kept kindergartens, Oxfam workers said.
"What we saw really shook all of us," Parker said. "We saw very severely malnourished children and we are quite sure that some of these children will not survive."

While international agencies had arranged for emergency high-protein milk and biscuits to be supplied to children aged up to five, food shortages remained acute and symptoms of hunger were appearing among the wider population, she said.
"There are a very large number of adults who are slipping into malnourishment as well, because of the very long-term lack of food in the system," she said.

North Korean state media reported at the weekend that some drought-hit areas had received more than 100 mm (four inches) of rain, but Parker said one-off showers were of little help to farmers struggling to keep their crops alive.

The drought had affected 11 of North Korea's 12 provinces, with temperatures averaging 33 degrees Celsius (91.4 degrees Fahrenheit) since June 1, well above the normal average of 28C (82.4F), Oxfam workers said.
While North Korea remains one of the world's most secretive societies, aid agencies have in recent months reported an easing of controls on their access to famine-threatened areas.
"The way in which we are able to see what is happening has increased enormously," Parker said.

"I think that's really just due to the fact that the North Koreans are so acutely aware now of the impossible situation that they are in," she said. "They know they are going to be dependent on international aid for some time to come.
